newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat visits Israel but negotiations difficult.
newsitem.headline: Arafat visits Israel but negotiations difficult.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat paid his first public visit to Israel on Tuesday in a symbolic display of a renewed Israeli-Palestinian search for peace.

Although the former guerrilla leader expressed disappointment with Israel's approach to the latest peace talks before leaving Gaza by helicopter, he was smiling broadly when met on arrival in Caesarea by Israeli President Ezer Weizman.
Weizman, whose role is largely ceremonial, had announced plans two months ago to invite Arafat when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was still refusing to see the Palestinian leader.
But the meeting, which was only scheduled on Monday, was timed to coincide with the resumption of peace talks after an emergency summit in Washington last week.
Violence sparked by Netanyahu's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Islamic sites in Jerusalem last month cost the lives of 59 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.

Weizman greeted Arafat, wearing his trademark khaki uniform and chequered keffiyeh, at the entrance to his whitewashed villa in the seafront community. Arafat's smile contrasted with the grim expression seen when beside Netanyahu at the summit.
The Palestinian leader's only previous visit to Israel -- a condolence call on the widow of assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin last November -- was at night and without advance announcement.
"Negotiations will be the instrument for solving all our differences," Arafat told reporters, trying to put the violence of the past weeks behind.

A spokesman for Netanyahu, who had been embarrassed by the original invitation to Arafat, told Israel Radio he expected the Weizman-Arafat meeting would touch upon Israel's long-delayed troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron.
"We welcome any effort or contribution that can advance the peace process and Israel's interests in it," Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said of Weizman inviting Arafat to his home.

Despite the Weizman meeting and an easing of Israeli military restrictions in the West Bank, Palestinians expressed little optimism about the Hebron talks that opened on Monday with a U.S. appeal for urgent progress.
Palestinian negotiators said basic differences had surfaced at the opening session of the talks on the occupied West Bank city that had been agreed at the Washington summit.

The government that Netanyahu defeated in May elections had signed a commitment to thin forces in Hebron, a city of 100,000 Arabs with 400 militant Jewish settlers in the centre, nearly seven months ago.
"The Israeli side is still working to cancel the agreement which threatens to undermine the whole peace process," Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters.

Arafat, who wants Israel to honour the original agreement with only minor adjustments, told reporters in Gaza asking about the Monday session: "I'm sorry it was not positive but we hope something new will happen today."
Israel, while maintaining the changes it wants do not amount to reopening the Hebron agreement, says it wants better security for the Jewish settlers in the city.
Naveh said Israel would "continue to clarify our security needs" in the ongoing negotiations and could not give a date for concluding the negotiations.
